story.headline: A global slide in AI-linked stocks was the week's big story, sending gold to its worst week in eight months. The yen gained while the Aussie fell hardest, and a December Fed hike still looks likely.

reads.policy: A December Fed hike is still seen as likely, and several officials argued for more, but the stock slide made bigger steps less likely. The European Central Bank and Bank of England are also expected to hike, while Australia's job losses make another Reserve Bank of Australia hike unlikely. US rates still look set to rise further than most, which keeps supporting the dollar.
reads.growth: Australia lost jobs for a second month, a blow to the Aussie. UK shoppers spent more than expected, partly by stocking up. A global stock slide raises worries that growth will slow, which usually hits commodity currencies hardest.
reads.inflation: Inflation is still well above target almost everywhere, which keeps most central banks leaning toward hikes. UK core prices held steady while euro-area core prices firmed. US households expect a little less inflation than earlier this month, which eased bets on the Fed slightly.
reads.risk: Stocks fell hard around the world as worries about AI spending spread, and the S&P 500 ended the week more than 10% below its October record. Money moved into US government bonds, the yen and the franc. The Aussie and kiwi, which suffer most when markets get nervous, fell to near multi-year lows.
reads.tot: Gold had its worst week in about eight months, which weighs on the Aussie. Oil fell for a third week as Gulf supply kept flowing despite attacks on tankers, which takes support away from the Canadian dollar and helps energy buyers such as Japan and the euro area.
reads.positioning: The latest weekly figures show hedge funds have turned slightly against the dollar after betting on it, while still betting against the euro, the kiwi, the franc and, most strongly, the Canadian dollar. They still bet on the pound and the Aussie, where big long-term investors take the opposite side. Where the two groups disagree, a surprise could set off a fast unwind.
reads.fiscal: France's debts, flagged by the European Central Bank as a risk, keep weighing on the euro. Record US government borrowing still keeps long-term US borrowing costs high, though they slipped below 5% as money rushed into bonds during the stock slide.

fed.summary: The Federal Reserve held rates on October 28 with two officials voting to hike, and most officials now expect more hikes. A deeper US stock slide and cooler inflation expectations trimmed December bets a little, but a hike is still the likely next move.
fed.priced: December: hike very likely, though a little less certain after the stock slide. More hikes expected next year.
fed.why: US inflation is running at about twice the Fed's 2% goal. US consumers now expect prices to rise more slowly, and a falling stock market gives officials a reason to go carefully.
fed.watch: US core inflation for October on Wednesday, November 25 at 7:30 AM CT, then the Beige Book at 1:00 PM CT. The decision is December 9.

boc.summary: The Bank of Canada raised rates to 2.50% in October and said more may be needed. October inflation held at 3.1% with core prices near 2%, so a December hike now looks less likely than not.
boc.priced: December: hold more likely, with a hike a bit under even odds.
boc.why: Energy is lifting headline inflation, but core prices are calm and the economy is shedding jobs, so the bank can afford to wait.
boc.watch: Governor Tiff Macklem speaks Tuesday, November 24 at 11:25 AM CT, and oil prices. The decision is December 9.

rbnz.summary: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand held at 2.75% in October in a narrow vote. Rising unemployment has made a December hike less certain, and the kiwi has fallen to its lowest since 2020.
rbnz.priced: December: hike possible but not fully expected.
rbnz.why: Inflation pressures argue for a hike, but unemployment at its highest since 2015 argues for waiting. Governor Anna Breman gave no clear signal on December in her latest speech.
rbnz.watch: The official election result on Friday, November 27 and the next dairy price auction. The decision is December 9.

ecb.summary: The European Central Bank held at 2.50% in October and a December hike is widely expected. Euro-area inflation is confirmed at 4.0%, but the euro sits just under $1.10 as US rates rise faster.
ecb.priced: December: hike widely expected, possibly the last for a while.
ecb.why: Euro-area inflation is about double the bank's goal and core prices are firming. Weak factories and France's debts, which the bank's stability report singled out, limit how far it can go.
ecb.watch: Euro-area business surveys on Monday, November 23 at 3:00 AM CT and the accounts of the October meeting on Thursday, November 26 at 6:30 AM CT. The decision is December 17.

boj.summary: The Bank of Japan holds at 1.25%, far below other major banks, and is expected to hike in December. Japan's October inflation came in a touch below forecast but stayed above the bank's 2% goal, which keeps that hike likely.
boj.why: Inflation has stayed above 2% for a second month, and the weak yen keeps pushing up import and food prices. The small summer contraction is the main reason to wait.
boj.watch: Tokyo's November inflation figures on Thursday, November 26 at 5:30 PM CT, and any sign Japan steps in near 160 yen. The decision is December 18.

rba.summary: The Reserve Bank of Australia raised rates to 4.85% on November 3, the highest among the major banks. Australia lost jobs in October and unemployment hit a five-year high, which supports the view that rates have peaked, and the Aussie is near its lowest in a year.
rba.priced: December: a hold expected. Some bets on cuts in 2027 are building.
rba.why: Inflation is still too high for most of the board, but the job market is clearly weakening. That makes a further hike unlikely and puts the timing of a first cut in question.
rba.watch: Australian inflation for October on Tuesday, November 24 at 6:30 PM CT. The decision is December 8.

boe.summary: The Bank of England raised Bank Rate to 4.00% on November 5 and said more may follow. UK shoppers spent more than expected in October, which supports a second hike in December, but the pound sits near its lowest this year as US rates rise faster.
boe.priced: December: a second hike more likely than not.
boe.why: High fuel costs from the Middle East conflict keep UK inflation near twice the bank's goal. Spending held up in October, although much of it was food stockpiling that may not last.
boe.watch: UK business surveys on Monday, November 23 at 3:30 AM CT, and talks by chief economist Huw Pill on Monday and Megan Greene on Tuesday. The decision is December 17.

snb.summary: The Swiss National Bank holds its rate at zero and can sell francs if they get too strong. Low Swiss inflation means no hike is in sight.
snb.why: Swiss inflation is low, so the bank has no reason to raise rates and some room to cut if the franc climbs.
snb.watch: Any flare-up in stock markets or the Gulf that sends money into the franc. The decision is December 10.

GBP.summary: The pound sits at the top of the board because UK interest rates are among the highest of the eight. Steady core inflation trimmed bets on another hike, and it ended the week near its lowest this year.

AUD.summary: The Aussie sits second on the board, thanks to the highest interest rates among the major central banks. Australia's October job losses suggest those rates have peaked, and it had the worst week of the eight as gold and stocks fell.

USD.summary: The dollar sits third on the board. High and rising US interest rates support it, while large budget deficits weigh a little. It touched its highest since April 2025 this week before a stock slide pulled US yields lower.

NZD.summary: The kiwi sits fourth, in the middle of the board. Firm prices for New Zealand's dairy exports help, but doubts over a December rate hike and a global stock slide have kept it near its lowest since 2020.

EUR.summary: The euro sits fifth, just below the middle of the board. Cheaper oil helps the euro area, but France's debts and rates below most of the others hold it back. It touched its weakest in about 18 months this week.

CAD.summary: The Canadian dollar sits sixth, in the lower half of the board. Falling oil prices hurt Canada's exports, and recent Canadian data has mostly missed forecasts. It is near its weakest against the US dollar in more than a year.

JPY.summary: The yen sits second from the bottom because Japanese interest rates are far below the others. A global stock slide and a likely December Bank of Japan hike gave it its first weekly gain in four, after the dollar came close to 160 yen.

CHF.summary: The franc sits at the bottom of the board. Swiss interest rates are the lowest of the eight and inflation is too low to need higher rates. A late-week stock slide sent safe-haven money into it, pulling the dollar off an 18-month high.
